claims.text: Enhanced elevated-temperature wear performance of HEA protective coatings is governed by thermally activated in-situ formation of a coherent, adherent oxide barrier.
The protective oxide layer is enriched in oxidation-resistant elements such as Cr and Al.
The oxide layer reduces direct substrate abrasion.
Formation of the oxide layer lowers the coefficient of friction.
Powder-metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 can serve as a dual-phase example HEA for the proposed coating test.
Changing the elevated-temperature wear-test atmosphere from air to argon will modulate oxide formation.
The proposed mechanism should be examined over approximately 400°C to 650°C.
The structural mediator is a continuous protective surface layer consisting of chromia, alumina, or spinel-type oxides.
At high temperature in an oxygen-containing environment, oxygen-affine HEA elements oxidize to form a thin, coherent oxide film.
The oxide film reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and adhesive wear.
At identical elevated-temperature loading, samples tested in air will form a protective oxide and have lower wear rates than samples tested in argon.
At identical elevated-temperature loading, samples tested in air will have lower coefficients of friction than samples tested in argon.
An inert atmosphere will prevent formation of the protective oxide barrier and consequently produce higher wear.
Significant protective oxide formation is minimal during room-temperature wear testing in air.
The mechanism should operate above approximately 400°C until oxide spallation or breakdown occurs.
The mechanism is limited to alloy compositions that favor formation of protective oxides.
Atmospheric elevated-temperature wear of AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 shows increased wear resistance due to formation of a protective oxide layer.
The coefficient of friction of AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 decreases slightly with increasing temperature.
